question: How much of the Allegro is already contained in the slow introduction?
intro: A repeated C in the timpani supports string lines climbing by semitone against descending winds. The ensuing Allegro turns those small motions into a sonata movement; the same Czech National Symphony Orchestra recording supplies all four movements in this set.

sections.label: Introduction · Un poco sostenuto
sections.mNote: opposing chromatic lines over repeated C

sections.label: Exposition · Allegro
sections.mNote: short motifs expand into the main argument

sections.label: Development · themes in new surroundings
sections.mNote: arpeggios and descending figures change key and function

sections.label: Retransition · the long ascent
sections.mNote: quiet preparation grows towards the return

sections.label: Recapitulation · a compressed return
sections.mNote: earlier themes return with altered proportions and home-key orientation

sections.label: Coda · withdrawal and Meno allegro
sections.mNote: chromatic motifs settle into a quiet C-major close

cues.title: Opposite directions over C
cues.text: Across the opening, the violins and cellos climb by semitone while winds and violas descend. Timpani repeat C beneath them. The bass stands still while the upper parts pull against one another.
cues.evidence: Simrock score p. 3 shows the contrary-motion opening and repeated C. The report places sustained high relative level at 0:00–0:35 and repeatedly identifies C in the bass; this describes the opening passage, not separate entrances.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Weight gives way to space
cues.text: The opening pressure gives way to separated, lighter gestures. Listen for the difference between a sustained orchestral line and notes that leave space around their attacks; both belong to the introduction’s argument.
cues.evidence: The strong boundary at 0:38 accompanies a fall from −10.2 dB at 0:35 to −23.5 dB at 0:40. The score changes to plucked string figures after the opening half-cadence; no individual pluck is aligned.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Karlsruhe, not Vienna
cues.text: Felix Otto Dessoff conducted the premiere in Karlsruhe on 4 November 1876. Brahms was forty-three; his First Symphony reached the public after the two serenades, the First Piano Concerto and the Haydn Variations.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s Boston Symphony note documents the premiere, age and preceding orchestral works: https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The introduction builds again
cues.text: A renewed swell brings the opening’s weight back into view. The small chromatic motions matter more than a new tune: the introduction keeps reworking the material with which it began.
cues.evidence: The score restates the opening material from bar 25. The report rises from −26.0 dB at 1:35 to −5.4 dB at 1:55, then withdraws after 2:05; this anchors the broad restatement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A pause before motion
cues.text: Through this quiet end of the introduction, keep the earlier climbing figure in mind. Brahms lets the texture thin before the Allegro turns its semitones and short-note rhythms into a much faster argument.
cues.evidence: The report shows a sustained withdrawal at 2:25–2:50, with the lowest pre-ending window at 2:45. The score ends its introduction with oboe and cello lines and dominant preparation before bar 38.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Allegro makes connections
cues.text: In the Allegro’s opening group, rising arpeggios coexist with the introduction’s chromatic figure. An arpeggio spreads a chord into successive notes; the semitone figure presses between adjacent pitches. Hear their different shapes working together.
cues.evidence: The marked rise between 2:50 and 2:55 supports the approximate Allegro boundary at 2:54. Bars 38–51 supply the motto and arpeggiated first theme; Hansen’s guide is used for bar descriptions, not its performance times.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three short notes persist
cues.text: Throughout the movement, listen for three short notes gathering into a longer arrival. The pattern can remain recognisable when the melody changes register or the orchestration becomes heavier.
cues.evidence: Mandel identifies the three-quaver motive and its relation to the introduction: https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor. This is a movement-wide rhythmic listening point, not a timestamped quotation of Beethoven.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The exposition opens space
cues.text: After the forceful opening group, the sound withdraws into more separated phrases. Keep following the bass through the thinning texture: a quieter passage can continue the harmonic motion instead of stopping it.
cues.evidence: Relative level drops from −10.5 dB at 4:15 to −24.9 dB at 4:25 and remains lower through 4:50. The note describes the measured thinning without assigning a precise chord or solo entrance.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Lyricism keeps the semitones
cues.text: The exposition’s gentler material does not abandon chromatic motion. Listen across its longer wind phrases for the same small intervals that sounded insistent in the introduction, now absorbed into a more connected melody.
cues.evidence: The second-theme region follows the quiet transition, approximately 4:45–5:35 here. Bars 121–156 combine the three-note chromatic figure with oboe and clarinet phrases; the report’s changing level anchors a passage, not a single entry.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Listen below the melody
cues.text: Across the quieter phrases, distinguish the line from the repeated notes underneath it. Brahms can keep the accompaniment moving while a wind melody stretches across the beat; a sustained top note does not mean that the phrase has stopped.
cues.evidence: The score’s second-theme group places repeated viola notes and moving supporting parts beneath wind melody. The report has quiet windows around 5:35–5:55; no particular sustained pitch is claimed at 5:42.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Closing figures gather weight
cues.text: The end of the exposition gathers force through descending figures and overlapping parts. Follow the direction of the phrases as well as their volume: falling lines can contribute to an accumulating climax.
cues.evidence: Bars 157–188 provide the descending closing material. A strong boundary at 6:04 precedes elevated relative level through 6:35, supporting this placement before the development boundary at 6:40.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A different tonal starting point
cues.text: The development begins by moving the first theme’s arpeggio into B major, rather than settling in the exposition’s E♭ region. The familiar shape survives; its harmonic setting changes the direction of the argument.
cues.evidence: The score’s second ending at bar 189 begins the development in B. The report has a strong 6:40 boundary and B-major estimates at 6:40–6:50, followed by a withdrawal at 6:55; the score supplies the key, not the estimate alone.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fragments instead of whole themes
cues.text: In the development, listen for a theme’s beginning continuing without its original ending. A rising arpeggio or a descending fragment can be repeated at another pitch and passed between strings and winds before a complete melody returns.
cues.evidence: This summarises the development’s treatment of arpeggios and closing-theme fragments, bars 189–272, described in Hansen’s score guide. It does not align a specific exchange to 7:36.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Schumann’s public expectation
cues.text: Robert Schumann’s 1853 article “Neue Bahnen” presented the twenty-year-old Brahms as a major new composer. It appeared more than twenty years before this symphony’s premiere, making Brahms’s first orchestral symphony a long-awaited event rather than a debut from an unknown musician.
cues.evidence: Malte Krasting’s Berliner Philharmoniker note discusses Schumann’s 1853 article and the delayed symphony: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor-op-68/. The site’s Brahms biography and influence edge give the same chronology.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A bass that refuses to leave
cues.text: The preparation for the return makes a prolonged G in the bass a source of tension. G is the dominant of C: repeated or sustained, it can keep the home key in prospect while the upper parts continue moving.
cues.evidence: Bars 273–293 sustain the dominant preparation. The report repeatedly identifies G in the bass from 8:40 to 9:15 while relative level falls towards 9:05. This supports a broad pedal passage, not a chord-by-chord transcription.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A long ascent from quiet
cues.text: The return is prepared by a rising accumulation rather than a clean break. Listen for the distance between the quiet beginning of the buildup and its much heavier continuation; the bass and upper lines contribute to the same increasing pressure.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −30.4 dB at 9:05 through −17.3 at 9:30 to −6.7 at 9:50. Strong boundaries at 9:20 and 9:38 fall inside the score-informed retransition estimate.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A return without a reset
cues.text: Near the return, the repeated rhythmic figure and climbing semitones are already in motion. Brahms does not need to clear the texture before recovering the opening Allegro material: the preparation itself grows into the recapitulation.
cues.evidence: Bars 321–343 carry the retransition into a modified opening motto, without its original initial C attack. The report’s sustained high-level region at 9:50–10:25 supports a continuous span, with the formal seam estimated at 10:26.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first group returns compressed
cues.text: The recapitulation restores the first theme but shortens its route onwards. Listen for familiar material doing less preparatory work than before: a return can change the proportions while preserving the movement’s recognisable figures.
cues.evidence: The score’s recapitulation starts at bar 340 and omits part of the exposition’s first group before its transition. Its placement near 10:26 is estimated from the long preceding buildup and the renewed withdrawal at 11:05–11:20.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The return also withdraws
cues.text: The returned opening group gives way to a quieter stretch. Compare this retreat with the exposition’s earlier one: the contrast between full orchestral weight and lighter phrases remains a structural signpost.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −8.0 dB at 11:00 to −21.2 at 11:10 and −25.8 at 11:20. The note compares measured contours without claiming that the two passages are identical.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A friend found it harsh
cues.text: The surgeon Theodor Billroth, a close friend and chamber-music partner of Brahms, admired the finale but found the first movement’s material too defiant and harsh. Early responses did not treat the four movements as having one uniform character.
cues.evidence: Mandel reports Billroth’s contrasting judgements of the first movement and finale: https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor. His chamber-music friendship is described in the site’s Brahms biography.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Another closing accumulation
cues.text: The later closing group again moves from reduced sound towards a stronger orchestral statement. Keep the descending figures in mind: the movement can increase its force without replacing them with a new theme.
cues.evidence: The score returns the closing theme in C minor from bar 430. The report’s boundary at 12:46 and rise from −28.2 dB at 12:40 to −11.0 at 12:45 support the approximate closing-group placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cadences do not finish everything
cues.text: The forceful cadential gestures are not yet the ending. Listen past each apparent arrival for the next continuation; Brahms extends the closing argument before allowing the tempo and orchestral weight to subside.
cues.evidence: Bars 450–474 extend the closing material through repeated gestures and an avoided arrival. Relative level stays high through 13:35, then drops sharply at 13:40; this anchors the late extension and withdrawal.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A quieter kind of coda
cues.text: The coda reduces the orchestral pressure and lets the chromatic figure become a more connected phrase. The later instruction Meno allegro — less fast — changes the pace of the closing argument instead of adding a final burst of speed.
cues.evidence: The score begins its coda at bar 475 and marks Meno allegro at bar 495. The report drops from −7.6 dB at 13:35 to −20.3 at 13:40, then remains mostly lower through 14:35; individual bars are not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Major is a quiet destination
cues.text: The closing pages move towards C major rather than ending in the movement’s prevailing minor. Listen for the major-key resolution as a change in harmony, not a requirement for a louder ending.
cues.evidence: The score closes in C major. The report’s final sustained region is compatible with C major, and relative level rises briefly at 14:40–14:50 before withdrawing; no precise first major chord is asserted.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Release after the argument
cues.text: The last chords leave room for their resonance. Compare this ending with the opening’s repeated timpani C: the same tonal centre can support pressure at the beginning and rest at the close.
cues.evidence: The report falls to −34.5 dB at 15:05, just before the 909.2-second file ends. The comparison concerns the score’s opening and closing C, not an isolated final-note onset.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

transitions.title: A held expectation becomes rhythmic motion
transitions.how: The introduction settles onto dominant preparation after its exposed wind and cello phrases. The Allegro answers with a low C and an accelerated version of the chromatic motto, then places the rising first-theme arpeggio above it. The tempo changes, but the semitone motion and short-note rhythm have already been introduced; the fast movement grows from the slow one rather than replacing its materials.
transitions.evidence: Bar 38 supplies the Allegro join. Relative level rises sharply between 2:50 and 2:55 after the quietest introduction windows. The 174-second anchor is approximate, not bar-aligned.

transitions.title: The closing descent leads to B
transitions.how: After the closing group’s hammered thirds, a descending link leads to B rather than returning directly to C. In the written second ending, the first theme’s arpeggio reappears in B major. Its contour supplies continuity while the new tonal position opens the development. The texture soon withdraws, leaving room for quieter exchanges between the strings and individual winds.
transitions.evidence: Bar 189, second ending, is the score reference. The strong 6:40 boundary, B-major estimates at 6:40–6:50 and level fall at 6:55 support the passage placement; the full repeat scheme has not been aligned bar by bar.

transitions.title: The dominant becomes a rising preparation
transitions.how: The development’s repeated G bass first holds the music in suspense. From that quiet preparation, rising chromatic bass figures and answering upper parts begin a longer accumulation. Horn rhythm and string motion preserve the opening’s motives while their register and weight increase. This is a retransition: a passage whose function is to make the return both expected and delayed.
transitions.evidence: The score’s extended retransition begins at bar 294 after the G pedal. The report places the low point at 9:05, followed by rising level and strong boundaries at 9:20 and 9:38; 9:10 marks the broad preparation, not its first notated bar.

transitions.title: The buildup grows into its own return
transitions.how: Brahms keeps the chromatic motto moving through the join. The recapitulation omits the exposition’s initial low C and takes over within the continuing harmonic sequence, so the first-theme return is not a fresh start after silence. The restored arpeggios confirm the thematic return; the altered approach and shortened first group prevent the exposition from simply being replayed.
transitions.evidence: Hansen describes the elided motto at bar 340 and first theme at bar 343. The report has continuous high relative level through 10:25 and a later withdrawal; 10:26 is a score-proportional estimate rather than a novelty-derived bar onset.

transitions.title: Hammered thirds soften into a final phrase
transitions.how: The closing extension diverts an expected arrival and then reduces the hammered thirds to quiet pizzicato figures. Above them, the rising semitone motto becomes a longer string phrase. The later Meno allegro lets winds and strings exchange that figure at a slower pace, and the final harmony settles in C major. Reduced texture, not a new closing theme, changes the function of familiar material.
transitions.evidence: Bars 475–511 supply the coda, Meno allegro and major close. Relative level drops sharply at 13:40 after the 13:35 crest; this supports the 820-second coda boundary, with later tempo and harmonic events left passage-level.

source.title: Brahms, Symphony No. 1, Simrock first-edition full score, plate 7957 (1877)
source.locator: Movement I, pp. 3–26; opening inspected directly. Later textures follow the score’s bar descriptions in Kelly Dean Hansen’s Op. 68 guide. Entries are representative passage snapshots, not continuous or ear-checked player tracking; section anchors follow this recording’s analysis.

timeline.note: Opening: rising string lines oppose descending winds over the repeated C foundation.
The lighter introduction passage exchanges plucked string figures over supporting wind harmony.
After the renewed introduction crest, the score exposes an oboe-led line with wind support.
The later introduction passes the exposed line to cellos against quiet upper strings.
The Allegro combines the violin arpeggio with the chromatic motto in lower parts.
The gentler second-theme region foregrounds connected wind phrases and repeated inner-string notes.
The development relocates the first-theme arpeggio, then reduces the texture for wind and string exchanges.
The long retransition builds from rising bass patterns and answering upper strings.
The returning first group restores the arpeggio with fuller wind support.
The coda softens the hammered thirds into plucked accompaniment beneath a connected violin phrase.
The slower closing span exchanges the chromatic figure between winds and strings.

composer.epithet: A composer who made a small interval generate a large form, and let conflicting rhythms keep a familiar melody unsettled.
facts: Piano with Otto Friedrich Willibald Cossel; piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen in Hamburg
Seasonal work in Detmold, 1857–59; Vienna Singakademie, 1863–64; Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde concerts, 1872–75
Based in Vienna; summer composition in Baden-Baden, Pörtschach, Mürzzuschlag and Bad Ischl
Four symphonies, four concertos, chamber music, piano music, songs and choral works; no opera
composer.background:
Brahms was born in Hamburg, the son of a professional musician, Johann Jakob Brahms, who played several instruments, and Christiane Nissen, a seamstress. His father supplied an introduction to practical music-making; Otto Friedrich Willibald Cossel and Eduard Marxsen gave him systematic piano and composition lessons. The young Brahms played for income and learned the trade from inside, accompanying, arranging and performing. Marxsen’s teaching connected keyboard technique with the study of Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. Those composers supplied working materials: Brahms’s later scores are full of old procedures subjected to new rhythmic pressure.

In 1853 he toured with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi and met Joseph Joachim, who became a lifelong collaborator. Joachim sent him to Robert and Clara Schumann in Düsseldorf. Robert’s article “Neue Bahnen”, published that October, announced the twenty-year-old as a major new figure before his music was widely available. The endorsement opened publishers’ doors and imposed an awkward expectation of scale. His early piano sonatas, already orchestral in weight and contrast, could be treated as promises of symphonies he had not yet written. Brahms responded by publishing selectively and destroying much of the work he did not wish to preserve.
